A.explanation: This describes the behaviour of most alpha-particles that miss nuclei, not why this one head-on gold nucleus recoils slowly.

B.explanation: Electrostatic repulsion explains why the alpha-particle is deflected, but equal and opposite forces act on both so it does not explain the different recoil speeds.

C.explanation: A gold nucleus of about 197 u is much more massive than an alpha-particle of 4 u, so the same momentum change gives it a much smaller speed from $v = p/m$.

D.explanation: The alpha-particle does slow down as repulsion does negative work on approach, but this does not by itself explain the small speed given to the gold nucleus.

hints: Notice the question asks about one head-on collision where the alpha-particle rebounds, and compares the recoil speed of the gold nucleus with the recoil speed of the alpha-particle.
Think about conservation of momentum in the collision: the impulse on the gold nucleus is equal and opposite to the impulse on the alpha-particle.
Use $p = mv$ to ask how the same size of momentum change produces very different speeds when the gold mass of about 197 u and the alpha mass of 4 u are compared.
walkthrough: Identify the event: a single alpha-particle hits a gold nucleus head-on and reverses direction, so momentum is exchanged between the two during the short repulsion.

State the governing rule: total momentum is conserved, so the change in momentum $\Delta p$ gained by the gold nucleus is equal in magnitude and opposite in direction to the change in momentum of the alpha-particle.
Compare the inertias: the gold nucleus mass is about 50 times the alpha-particle mass, since gold is about 197 u and an alpha-particle is 4 u.
Use $v = p/m$ for the recoil: for a given size of $\Delta p$, speed is inversely proportional to mass, so the much larger mass must move with a much smaller speed.
Therefore the small recoil speed of the gold nucleus is explained by its much greater mass. This is option C.
